title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
formal:
For every fixed pair of integers \(a,b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized data structure that maintains the exact canonical minimum spanning forest of the graph below, with polynomial preprocessing and space and polylogarithmic worst-case time for each edge insertion or deletion? For every valid update sequence \(\sigma\) of length \(T\le n^a\) fixed independently of its randomness, require
\[\Pr_R\bigl[\widehat F_t=F(G_t)\text{ for every }0\le t\le T\bigr]\ge1-n^{-b}.\]
The event also requires every edge-change report to be valid as defined below. Here \(G_t\) is the graph after update \(t\), \(F(G_t)\) is its specified exact forest, and \(\widehat F_t\) is reconstructed from the reported edge changes. Each update must finish within its time bound on every execution, including executions on which the answer is wrong. The data structure receives no future updates in advance.
definitions:
Graph and updates. Fix an integer \(n\ge2\), with labelled vertices \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is simple and undirected: no loops or parallel edges. Initially \(G_0\) has no edges. An insertion supplies distinct endpoints \(u,v\) of an absent edge and an integer weight \(w\in\{1,\ldots,n^4\}\); a deletion supplies the endpoints of a present edge. A weight stays fixed until its edge is deleted. Reinsertion may assign a different weight. A valid sequence respects these rules at every prefix; disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and repeated insertions after deletions are allowed. Vertices are never inserted or deleted. The exponent four is the retained concrete choice of polynomial weight range.

Exact target and ties. A spanning forest has one spanning tree in each connected component, with an isolated vertex contributing no edges. Its cost is the sum of its edge weights, and a minimum spanning forest minimizes that sum. To specify one answer when several forests have the same cost, order edges by the triple \((w,\min(u,v),\max(u,v))\), in increasing lexicographic order. Define \(F(G)\) by starting with no edges, scanning the present edges in this order, and retaining an edge exactly when adding it does not create a cycle. This is the canonical minimum spanning forest; the scan defines the target and is not a required implementation. In particular \(F(G_0)=\varnothing\).

Required output. After each update, before receiving the next one, report a list \(D_t\) of forest edges removed and a list \(A_t\) of forest edges added, using unordered endpoint pairs represented with their smaller endpoint first. Starting from \(\widehat F_0=\varnothing\), the reported forest is \(\widehat F_t=(\widehat F_{t-1}\setminus D_t)\cup A_t\). On a correct execution these lists must be exactly \(F(G_{t-1})\setminus F(G_t)\) and \(F(G_t)\setminus F(G_{t-1})\), respectively. Each contains at most one edge for a single valid update. Printing all current tree edges is not required. Duplicate or invalid reports count as a correctness failure; they never excuse exceeding the time or space bound. No later query or background computation may postpone completing the report.

Machine and costs. Use a classical sequential word RAM, with word length \(w_n=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for some fixed positive integer \(\lambda\) chosen with the data structure. Unit-cost operations are direct or indirect word reads and writes; word comparisons, branches and copies; addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w_n}\); integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor; bitwise Boolean operations; and shifts with zero fill and truncation to one word. A shift by at least the word length produces zero. One instruction may generate one independent uniformly random word. Larger integers require multiple words and their actual operations are charged. Endpoints and allowed weights occupy a constant number of words. Addressable memory cells contain words and have word-sized addresses. Input reading, output writing, random generation, memory access and all computation count. There is no rank oracle, free query to another graph algorithm, arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, parallel computation or uncharged lookup table.

Uniformity and resource bounds. For each fixed \(a,b\), choose one finite program, constants \(K\ge1\), integers \(C,D\ge1\), and \(\lambda\). These choices are independent of \(n\) and of the sequence. On input \(n\), initialization of the empty graph finishes within \(Kn^D\) steps and uses at most \(Kn^D\) words; all later memory use has the same bound. Initialized tables must be computed within this preprocessing budget. There is no advice or precomputed table varying with \(n\). For every valid sequence in the stated horizon and every realization of all random choices, update \(t\) finishes in at most
\[K\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^C\]
steps, including its report. Choose the word-length constant large enough to address the permitted memory. Randomness may be used in preprocessing and updates. The parameters \(a,b\) tune the allowable polynomial horizon and failure probability; the program and constants may depend on them. No uniform bound on that dependence is requested.

Probability convention. The entire input sequence is fixed before the data structure draws any random bits, so it is an oblivious sequence. The probability is over all random words \(R\), including initialization, and covers simultaneous correctness of every report throughout the sequence. Separate per-update probability bounds without a simultaneous bound are insufficient. The time and memory bounds themselves have no exceptional random outcomes. This is the retained Monte Carlo formulation: a small probability of a wrong answer is permitted, whereas an always-correct deterministic data structure would be a stronger positive answer.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, specify the programs for every fixed \(a,b\), their resource constants and randomization. Prove initialization, exact canonical forest maintenance, online reporting, worst-case time and space on every random execution, and the simultaneous probability bound for every valid oblivious sequence of length at most \(n^a\).

A negative answer must refute the stated quantified claim: for some fixed \(a,b\), no allowed uniform program and constants meet all requirements. It must cover randomized data structures with polynomial preprocessing and space in this word-RAM model. Failure of one technique or one logarithmic exponent, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an impossibility limited to a more restrictive access model does not suffice. A conditional lower bound must retain its assumptions and does not by itself refute this unconditional proposition.

Amortized polylogarithmic time, subpolynomial worst-case time, an expected-time bound alone, an approximate forest or a deferred expensive query does not meet the criterion. A result with probabilistic time bounds needs an explicit conversion satisfying the stated hard time cap and simultaneous correctness guarantee. A rank-query count or parallel span is not the sequential running time specified here.
why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.

importance.reason: One of the main unresolved worst-case update barriers in dynamic graph algorithms, closely connecting connectivity, weighted optimization, sparsification and expander maintenance.

progress.text: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup establish deterministic \(O(\log ^{4} n)\) amortized minimum-spanning-forest updates.
Holm–Rotenberg–Wulff-Nilsen improve amortized bounds; the \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) option uses randomized priority queues in the stated RAM model.
Nanongkai–Saranurak–Wulff-Nilsen give Las Vegas subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability.
Chuzhoy and coauthors obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case updates via deterministic expander decomposition.

Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s SODA paper gives expected polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity maintenance; its weighted extension is \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate with inverse-\(\varepsilon\) overhead.
De Vos–Grilnberger give logarithmically many rank queries per dynamic minimum-weight-base update, without a corresponding RAM update-time guarantee.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Inspected primary sources retain the gap between exact polylogarithmic amortized updates and exact subpolynomial worst-case updates. The SODA 2026 weighted extension is approximate, and ESA 2026 minimum-weight-base maintenance counts rank queries without bounding their implementation time. No matching exact polylogarithmic worst-case RAM resolution was found in the bounded source search; cited proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all \(n- 1\) tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic \(O(\log^4 n)\) amortized update bound. Amortization bounds the total cost across a sequence and permits individual updates to be much slower. The present target requires the current answer within the same polylogarithmic time budget after every single update, including a deletion chosen to expose a difficult replacement search.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain a Las Vegas algorithm: its answers are always correct, while each update has subpolynomial time in expectation and with high probability. These probability guarantees concern time. This card instead places a hard limit on time and allows a small probability of an incorrect forest. The two conventions must be distinguished even before comparing their asymptotic bounds.

Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case time for exact dynamic MSF. Subpolynomial remains weaker than polylogarithmic: \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\), for example, grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of \(n\) but faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\). Thus the deterministic theorem is a major improvement without meeting this card’s sharper running-time target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to \(\log (U)/\varepsilon\) for weights in \([1,U]\). The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

The dependence on \(\varepsilon\) prevents reading the approximate theorem as an exact polylogarithmic-time result. Integer forest costs differ by at least one, but a forest may have total weight as large as \((n-1)n^4\). Requiring multiplicative error small enough to certify exact cost in every instance introduces a polynomial, rather than polylogarithmic, overhead in the displayed guarantee. Exact cost would also still have to respect this card’s fixed choice among tied optima.

The ESA 2026 paper on dynamic matroids gives a deterministic algorithm maintaining a minimum-weight base with \(O(\log N)\) rank queries per update, where \(N\) is the matroid ground-set size. A rank query asks for the maximum size of an independent subset of an arbitrary supplied set. For a graph this requires determining the largest forest inside that edge set. The paper expressly distinguishes its oracle-query count from update time: it does not bound the cost of implementing these rank queries on a concrete matroid. Its proposition therefore does not settle the ordinary RAM problem here.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

sentences: The data structure receives insertions and deletions of weighted edges in an initially empty simple graph.
After every update it must report the changes to the exact minimum spanning forest with fixed tie-breaking.
The target combines a hard polylogarithmic update-time cap with simultaneous high-probability correctness over every polynomial-length oblivious sequence.
A complete Lean proof must cover the charged word-RAM computation, polynomial initialization and space, and all program and probability quantifiers, or refute the full allowed class.
Amortized bounds, subpolynomial worst-case bounds, approximate forests and logarithmic rank-query counts do not settle this exact maintenance question.

source_formulation.text: The card preserves the previously selected randomized, oblivious-adversary, exact weighted-forest question, its importance score, the weight range \(\{1,\ldots,n^4\}\), canonical tie-breaking and polynomial sequence horizon. The original imported ICALP 2021 link concerned matching and was already identified as a citation mismatch; the MSF target is grounded instead in the sources listed here. The present review makes the standard RAM convention and probability/resource quantifiers explicit without adding deterministic or adaptive-adversary requirements.
